fields.text:
`docs/guide/orchestration.md` ("A verify suite is a land-time gate, not a
standing regression suite") states three prohibitions:

- Don't run another task's already-landed verify suite.
- Don't edit a landed task's verify suite.
- Coverage that must survive belongs in the project's own test suite.

The rule is documented and was still violated three times in one session
(E-1901), including by a session whose handoff explicitly named
`endless guide orchestration`. It was then violated twice more in E-1889, by a
session that had read the same principle in its own task's analysis field on
its first tool call. Documentation is the wrong layer: a rule that must be read
gets skipped, and the skip does not feel like a violation — running an existing,
runnable-looking script feels like diligence.

Put the enforcement where the act happens, in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go`,
following the `blockPlanFileWriteIfApplicable` precedent already in that file
(same shape, same class of problem: a path that must not be hand-edited).

## Both suite forms, from day one

A suite exists in two forms and the guard must know both, or it goes blind
exactly when the project migrates:

| Form | Path | Run by |
|------|------|--------|
| script (current) | `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` | `./tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` |
| manifest (settled destination) | `.endless/tasks/e-<n>/verify.toml` | `endless task verify <id>` |

Both paths write the id lowercase. The manifest directories were uppercase
until they were renamed and `verify.Discover` was taught to compare ids
normalized (`verify.NormalizeTaskID`); the manifest's own `task` field remains
the canonical `E-NNNN` display form. Because an uppercase directory still
resolves, the id-extraction predicate here must accept either casing rather
than assuming the lowercase convention holds on disk.

Building the manifest arm now is not speculation. Two manifests already exist,
`endless task verify` already discovers and runs them, and the guide already
names `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml` as the settled form. Shipping a
script-only guard would mean re-opening this task the moment the migration
lands — the precise failure mode this task exists to prevent.

### What must NOT be blocked

- **`.endless/verify.toml` at the project root.** Same filename, one level up,
  and it is not a per-task suite — it carries shared `setup`/`teardown`/`seed`/
  `needs` composing beneath every task manifest. The predicate keys on the
  `.endless/tasks/<id>/` segment, not on the basename.
- **The tests a manifest points AT.** A manifest is a pointer, never a
  re-description: its `[[check]]` entries select native `gotest`/`pytest` tests
  living in `internal/...` and `tests/...`. Those are the project's durable
  suite and must stay freely editable forever. Blocking the manifest must not
  leak into blocking what it names — which is the whole reason the durable-test
  half of the prohibition works.

## Arm 1 — refuse the EDIT (the more damaging violation)

`PreToolUse` on Write/Edit/NotebookEdit: refuse a target matching either suite
form when task NNNN has landed AND is not this session's active task.

This is the arm that matters most. In E-1901 the suites were edited via Edit
without ever being run, so any guard living inside the script itself was inert.
Retrofitting the target string of a landed suite rewrites the record of what was
true when that task landed. In E-1889 the motive was more specific and worth
naming, because it will recur: the session's own change broke a landed suite's
assertion, and it edited the suite to keep it green. That is the failure this
arm must catch — the edit feels like fixing a break, not like falsifying a
record.

## Arm 2 — refuse the RUN

Same handler, Bash tool. Two invocation shapes, both refused for a landed,
non-active task:

- direct execution of `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` (any of `./x`, `bash x`,
  `sh x`, an absolute path);
- the manifest runner: `endless task verify <id>`, plus the `just verify <id>`
  wrapper that forwards to it.

The bare `endless task verify` with no id resolves to the session's own active
task and is always allowed — that is the pre-land gate doing its job.

A failure from a landed suite is meaningless by design, and acting on one
produces exactly the non-problem work E-1909 and E-1910 were (both declined).

## Landed-ness test

`session-query task-report --id N` already returns a `landed` bool; reuse it
rather than adding a second notion of landed-ness. Carve out the session's own
active task so the live, pre-land gate still runs and can still be authored.

A reopened task (`revisit`, per E-1889) is once again the session's active task,
so the carve-out restores its suite to writable and runnable without a special
case — reopening genuinely does put the task back in its pre-land window.

## Why no directory move, and no per-script retrofit

Moving `tests/tasks/` → `verify/tasks/` was considered and rejected: 123 task
rows and 141 commit messages embed the current path, all of them immutable
records, and `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml` is already the settled
destination as the runner matures — a move would churn the script form on its
way out. A rename also would not have prevented the violation: the scripts were
run because they existed and looked runnable, not because of the directory name.

Because the guard lives in the hook, NO existing suite is touched and every
landed suite of either form is covered the moment it ships. That is the point: a
per-script guard could only be added by editing landed suites, which is the
prohibition itself.

## Honest limits

- This cannot stop an agent from FILING a task about a landed suite — that is a
  judgment call no path pattern catches. E-1909/E-1910's decline reasons are the
  record for that case.
- It cannot stop a run laundered through an indirection the Bash matcher does
  not see (a wrapper script, `xargs`, a shell function). Arm 2 is a guardrail
  against the reflex, not a sandbox; Arm 1 is the arm that must be airtight.

## Verification

Unit tests on the pure predicate, covering both forms:

- path regex matches `tests/tasks/e-<n>-verify.sh` and
  `.endless/tasks/e-<n>/verify.toml`, in either casing (uppercase suite dirs
  still resolve), and not their neighbours;
- the project-root `.endless/verify.toml` is NOT matched;
- a path named by a manifest's `[[check]]` (e.g. `internal/monitor/x_test.go`)
  is NOT matched;
- landed + non-active → block; landed + active → allow; unlanded → allow;
- run-arm command parsing: the three script invocation shapes and
  `endless task verify <id>` / `just verify <id>` block; bare
  `endless task verify` allows;
- the block-response shape.

Mirror into the durable Go suite, not only into this task's verify script —
this task's own suite expires the moment it lands, which is the principle the
task is about.

Surfaced by E-1901, where all three prohibitions were violated in sequence:
six landed suites run, three edited (reverted in 54df9715), and two non-problem
tasks filed and declined. Re-confirmed by E-1889, where two landed suites were
edited (reverted in that branch before landing) and four were run as a standing
regression gate.

# E-1889 — Make reopening your own landed work the documented, tooled norm

Absorbs E-1890 (tooling counterpart). Every decision below is settled; there are
no open questions. Where a choice had a plausible alternative, the rejected one
is recorded so it is not relitigated.

## Problem

Agents reflexively file a new task for a bug they just introduced rather than
reopening the task that introduced it. The result is backlog growth.

A backlog is never free, on any project. Every filed task is a standing claim on
future attention: it must be read, re-read, and triaged past on every pass,
whether or not it is ever worked. A task filed reflexively does not defer the
cost of the discovery — it converts a small immediate cost into a recurring one.

On Endless itself that cost is currently visible as pending worktrees gating a
planned Python-to-Go port, but that is one instance of the cost, not the reason
for it.

Reproduced live in the E-1845 session: four tasks filed during one task, two of
which (E-1888, E-1891) turned out to be a single defect and had to be merged
afterward, and one of which (E-1894) rested on a category error and was retired.

The cause is not agent carelessness. The handoff template instructs exactly this
behavior.

## Settled decisions

| # | Decision | Rejected alternative |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `task reopen` is aligned to land `revisit`, like the other two reopen paths. Code change, not just docs. | Documenting the three paths' divergence as intentional. |
| 2 | Five templates get the full rewording; `brainstorm` keeps "file as new tasks" (that IS its deliverable) and gains only the root-cause test. | One wording across all six. |
| 3 | Mermaid gains `confirmed`/`assumed`/`completed` → `revisit`. `declined`/`obsolete` stay terminal in the diagram. | Drawing all five reopenable statuses. |
| 4 | Tooling folds into E-1889; E-1890 is absorbed and marked obsolete. | Keeping E-1890 for the recently-landed hint. |
| 5 | Claim promotion gains `revisit`. | Routing `spawn --reopen` through re-approval. |
| 6 | `_REOPEN_TO_REVISIT` narrows to E-1555's set; `declined`/`obsolete` are no longer implicitly revived. | Broadening `task reopen` to accept them. |
| 7 | Handoff uses the four-case bulleted form. | Compact prose; minimal edit. |
| 8 | `revisit` definition broadens to a two-case sentence. | Terse form; form with explicit pointer. |
| 9 | Guide pattern lives in `orchestration.md`, cross-referenced from `tasks.md`. | `tasks.md` only; `orchestration.md` with no pointer. |
| 10 | Verification splits by durability: behavior into the real suites, acceptance into the verify script. | Everything in one verify script. |
| 11 | `session resume --reopen` on `declined`/`obsolete` refuses loudly and names the explicit route. | Silently skipping the flip; a `--force` override. |

## A. Handoff templates

Under `internal` templatecmd templates handoff. Five files carry byte-identical
text at the noted lines: `todo.md.tmpl:12`, `bugfix.md.tmpl:14`,
`epic.md.tmpl:25`, `research.md.tmpl:14`, `respawn.md.tmpl:45`. Replace with:

```
4. Stay focused on E-{{.spawned_id}}. For anything you discover along the way:
   - Could it reasonably be done now, inside the work already underway? Do it —
     note it in the commit message, and add a `discovery` note to
     `endless task report`.
   - Is it a bug in work THIS session landed? Reopen that task
     (`endless task update E-NNN --status revisit`) and fix it there.
   - Otherwise file it (`--cleans-up E-{{.spawned_id}}`) and confirm before
     implementing.
   - Filing more than one? Check whether they share a root cause — file the
     cause, not each symptom.
```

"Report it" is spelled out deliberately: the earlier draft said only "do it,
and report it", which is the kind of vagueness that makes a bullet ignorable.
The two halves do different jobs — the commit message records WHAT changed, the
`discovery` note records THAT the session went beyond its brief. Without the
note the user has to read the diff to learn scope grew. `task report --json`
already accepts `{"kind": "discovery"}` and bounces entries it judges
ceremonial, so that filter — not the agent's judgment of significance — is the
guard against noise.

`respawn.md.tmpl` uses hyphen bullets with no step number; adapt the list marker
to match its surrounding style, keeping the four cases verbatim.

`brainstorm.md.tmpl:16` keeps its existing sentence — for a brainstorm, emitting
tasks and decisions IS the deliverable — and gains one line:

```
   Filing more than one? Check whether they share a root cause — file the
   cause, not each symptom.
```

## B. Canonical status lifecycle

Edit `docs/status-lifecycle.mmd`, then re-sync the three byte-identical copies
in `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `docs/guide/index.md`. Add:

```
    confirmed --> revisit: shipped work found wrong
    assumed --> revisit: shipped work found wrong
    completed --> revisit: shipped work found wrong
```

Keep the existing `confirmed --> [*]`, `assumed --> [*]`, `completed --> [*]`
edges — those statuses remain ordinary end states; the new edges say the door is
not locked.

`declined` and `obsolete` deliberately gain no edge (decision 6 removes the only
implicit path that revived them).

## C. `revisit` definition

`docs/guide/index.md`, the status table:

```
| `revisit` | Needs re-evaluation before it can proceed — either a partial plan
that no longer holds, or work that shipped and turned out wrong. Reopening your
own landed work lands here. |
```

The mermaid's existing `unplanned --> revisit: needs re-evaluation` label stays
as-is; the new edges carry the shipped-work case.

Note: the same table's `declined` row says "Requires `--reason`". Verified
correct — `--reason` is `task decline`'s flag, stored as outcome. Do not
"fix" it.

## D. Guide pattern — "Fix a bug in your own landed work"

New section in `docs/guide/orchestration.md`, near the existing `--reopen`
material (currently around the `task spawn --reopen` line). It must cover:

1. **The judgment.** A bug in work you just landed is not new work. Reopen the
   task that introduced it rather than filing a peer.
2. **The mechanics.** `task update <id> --status revisit`, then reuse the
   task's existing worktree rather than creating a second one for the same work.
3. **Re-verification.** The task's verify script still exists and still applies;
   re-run it rather than authoring a second one.
4. **The boundary.** When a genuinely separate task IS right — the discovery is
   new work the conversation surfaced, not a defect in what shipped.

One-line cross-reference from `tasks.md` under the status material, pointing
here.

## E. Code — reopen alignment

1. **`_reopen_task_core`** (`src/endless/task_cmd.py`, around the
   `new_status = "ready" if text_present else "unplanned"` line): always
   `revisit`. Keep returning `text_present` — callers use it for the message
   suffix — but stop branching status on it. Update the `reopen_item` docstring,
   which currently says "back to `ready` or `unplanned`".

2. **Five stale help/comment sites** assert the old target and must be updated
   in the same change: `task_cmd.py` at the spawn-reopen docstring, the
   `--reopen` help string, and the two reopen pre-step comments; plus the
   matching `--reopen` help text in `cli.py`.

3. **`_REOPEN_TO_REVISIT`** (`src/endless/session_cmd.py`): narrow to
   `{confirmed, assumed, completed}`, matching `_REOPENABLE_TERMINAL_STATUSES`.
   In `_resolve_resume`, refuse when `--reopen` targets a `declined`/`obsolete`
   task:

   ```
   Error: E-123 is 'declined' — a deliberate decision, not dormant work.
   Reviving it is an explicit act:
       endless task update E-123 --status revisit
   Then resume without --reopen.
   ```

   Follows the loud-failure-on-invalid-state convention used by the verb,
   maybe-parent, and db gates.

4. **Claim promotion** (`internal/monitor/session.go`): add `revisit` to the
   `status IN (...)` set. Without it, `task spawn --reopen` would bind a session
   and leave the task reading as not-started. The background-session gate is a
   separate check and is unchanged — background sessions remain restricted to
   `ready`.

## F. Code — three file-time hints

All three fire from `task add`. **Hints, never refusals** — sometimes a
genuinely separate task IS right, and the distinction needs human judgment.
Follow the existing gate/hint conventions.

1. **Recently landed.** When `--cleans-up X` names a task that the CURRENT
   session landed within 24h (join `task_landings` on `task_id` + `session_id`,
   filter `landed_at`), print: *"E-X was landed by this session Nh ago —

row `removed = 1`, so the id can never be re-minted and the FK-free rows that
deliberately outlive their task can never resurrect against unrelated work.

Absorbs E-1930, E-1931 and E-1932 (all closed `obsolete`).

Settled with the requester before filing; none of these are open.

| Question | Decision |

| A removed task's visibility | `task show <id>` renders it marked removed; `task list --removed` lists them; invisible everywhere else |
| Scope | Tasks only. Decisions and sessions have no reachable delete path, and decisions are being merged back into tasks |
| Read-filter mechanism | New `live_tasks` view; rewrite the 182 read sites to use it |

## Why the id can be re-minted today

`internal/events/executor.go:53` allocates with
`SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 FROM tasks`. Only the *highest* id is ever
re-freed — interior gaps are never refilled — so no historical backfill is
needed. Retaining the row keeps `MAX(id)` monotonic, which is the entire fix.

**The single most important constraint in this change: that allocation query
must keep reading `tasks`, never `live_tasks`.** Pointed at the view it would
stop seeing removed rows, `MAX(id)` would drop back, and ids would be reused
again — reintroducing the exact bug while appearing to fix it. Same for the
`decisions` allocator at `executor.go:93`, which this plan does not otherwise
touch.

at land time by `endless db apply-change`; the runner wraps it in
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` and records the `_schema_version` marker, so it runs once.

```sql
ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN removed INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS live_tasks AS
  SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE removed = 0;

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_tasks_removed ON tasks(removed);
```

Plus the one-shot data repair in §5, in the same transaction.

Per ED-1472 `schema.sql` is the single source of truth and must be edited to
declare the post-migration shape — the `removed` column on `tasks` (line 198),
the `live_tasks` view, and the index. The sandbox and tests build from
`schema.sql` and never apply change files, so a change file without the matching
`schema.sql` edit passes the migration and fails every fresh build.

`SELECT *` in the view is deliberate: it inherits future columns automatically.
If that proves fragile against `ALTER TABLE`, the fallback is an explicit column
list, which then has to be maintained alongside `schema.sql`.

## 2. Removal path — executor

`execTaskDeleted` in `internal/events/executor.go:780-830`.

Replace both DELETEs with UPDATEs:

- Non-cascade: `UPDATE tasks SET removed = 1 WHERE id = ?`
- Cascade: same `WITH RECURSIVE tree(id)` walk, `UPDATE tasks SET removed = 1
  WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM tree)`

Keep the existing `UPDATE tasks SET parent_id = NULL WHERE parent_id = ?`. Today
that re-roots the orphans; retaining the row would otherwise leave children
hanging off an invisible parent, so preserving it is what keeps the tree
readable.

Add what the FKs used to do and now will not:

```sql

UPDATE session_statuses SET active_task_id = NULL WHERE active_task_id = ?;
```

live state that would be a lie, and E-1856 shows `active_task_id` drift is not
hypothetical. Under `--cascade` these must run for every id in the tree, not
just the root.

`task_landings` was `ON DELETE CASCADE` and now simply will not fire. That is
the intended outcome — landing history is audit data, and the retained task row
is there to explain it. No code needed; note it in the change-file comment so a
future reader does not "fix" it.

```sql
DELETE FROM session_notices WHERE task_id = ? AND notified = 0;
```

Undelivered mail about a removed task is dead; filtering it on read would leave
it queued permanently. Delivered history is untouched. This is not an exception
to ED-1547 — a notice's own id is an internal row handle nobody refers to.

`execTaskBulkCleared` (`executor.go:865-885`) gets the identical treatment: the
`DELETE FROM tasks WHERE project_id = ? AND source_file = ?` becomes an UPDATE,
keeping its existing `parent_id` re-rooting. E-1915's reasoning applies — one
rule with no exemption beats two rules with a judgment call at the boundary.

they are. Refusing to remove a task that still has relations is orthogonal to
how the removal is then recorded.

## 3. Removal path — projector

`internal/events/projector.go:451,458` (task) and `:483` (bulk clear) must be
changed to match §2 exactly.

This is the rebuild path: it replays the whole ledger to rebuild the DB from
scratch. If the projector still replayed removal as a real DELETE while the
executor marked `removed = 1`, a rebuild would silently re-free every removed
id — the failure ED-1547 calls out by name, on a path nobody would think to
test. §6 verifies it explicitly.

occurrences:

| File | n |
|---|---|
| `src/endless/task_cmd.py` | 52 |
| `internal/web/queries.go` | 20 |
| `internal/events/executor.go` | 18 |
| `internal/monitor/session_status.go` | 13 |
| `internal/events/projector.go` | 10 |
| `internal/events/epic_derivation.go` | 5 |
| `internal/monitor/session.go`, `internal/monitor/triage_reads.go` | 4 each |
| `internal/monitor/task_report.go`, `src/endless/reconcile.py`, `src/endless/session_cmd.py` | 3 each |

missed rewrite leaks a removed task into `session status` and the monitor.

  SQLite views are not writable; these stay on the table.
- The removal path itself (§2, §3) — it must see and set rows the view hides.
- `task show <id>` and `task list --removed` (§5).
- The §5 repair sweep.
- `internal/schema/changes/*.sql`. Historical migrations are applied-once
  history, not live code; editing them rewrites the past.
- `src/endless/reconcile.py`'s orphan detection, if its purpose is finding rows
  whose task is gone. Decide per call site while reading it.

Test files were excluded from the counts and need the same pass.

## 5. CLI surface

only the emitted effect changes. Reword its output from "deleted" to "removed"
so the CLI stops claiming something it no longer does.

`task show <id>` resolves against `tasks`, not `live_tasks`, and renders a
removed task with a clear marker. This is the payoff for retaining the row: an
id that is a hole explains itself instead of erroring.

removed and live rows in one listing.

reused id — the row's timestamp predates its task's `created_at`:

```sql

   SELECT st.id FROM session_tasks st
```

no longer exists (harmless — they are what "outlives its task" means, and they
are already invisible through the view). `session_hidden_tasks`,
`session_notices` and `project_next_tasks` are clean, zero rows each, so the
sweep is one table. Re-measure at implementation time before running it.

1. `just build && just test`.
2. Remove a task in a sandbox DB; confirm the row survives with `removed = 1`,
   that it is absent from `task list`, `session status`, the monitor and the web
   dashboard, and that `task show <id>` renders it marked removed.
3. Confirm `MAX(id)` does not drop: remove the highest task, add a new one, and
   assert the new id is higher than the removed one. This is the regression the
   whole change exists to prevent.
4. Confirm `sessions.active_task_id` and `session_statuses.active_task_id` are
   nulled, and that `task_landings` rows survive.
5. Confirm pending `session_notices` for the removed task are gone and delivered
   ones remain.
6. **Rebuild the DB from the ledger and re-run checks 2 and 3.** This is the
   check that catches an executor/projector divergence; without it the change
   can look complete and still re-free every id on the next rebuild.
7. `task remove --cascade` on a parent: every descendant marked, every
   descendant's `active_task_id` pointers nulled.
8. Confirm the E-1915 relation guard and E-1927 bulk-clear guard still refuse.

payload.description: Surfaced while planning E-1929, which has to carry the import path through the removed-flag change. 'endless task import' loads a Claude plan file or JSON into the DB, with --replace bulk-clearing prior tasks from the same source file. It looks dormant: all 14 tasks with a source_file date from April 2026 across two plan files, 13 of the 14 are declined, and task.bulk_cleared has fired 5 times in the project's entire history. Plan attachment via 'task update --text' appears to have replaced the workflow it was built for. Note the CLI is 'task import --json', not the 'task import-json' named in a stale code comment. Decide: keep it, or retire it and drop the second task-delete path (task.bulk_cleared) along with its E-1927 guard, its executor and projector handlers, and the source_file column's reason for existing.

triage.rationale: The task poses a keep-or-retire decision without stating which way to go or what evidence would settle it, so the actual design work (making that call and scoping the retirement) hasn't happened yet.

payload.title: Block line numbers and other time-frozen specifics from durable task content
payload.description: ED-1073 already forbids time-frozen specifics — byte counts, file sizes, line numbers, sha hashes — and says to cite file or function names instead so the reader re-locates at pickup. It is violated routinely because nothing enforces it and two things undercut it: ED-1073's own text scopes the rule to the analysis field, so a literal reading does not reach a plan in text, a description, or an outcome; and the tasks guide describes text as a full implementation plan 'including approach, file paths, verification steps', which invites the thing the decision forbids. Three parts: extend the content gate that already refuses absolute paths in --description/--text so it also refuses file.ext:NNN and bare :NNN citations; widen ED-1073 to govern all durable content; and fix the guide's wording to say file and function names. Prompted by E-1929's plan, which cited line numbers throughout and goes stale as soon as anything else lands.

1. Remove a task — the row survives with `removed = 1`.
2. It is absent from `task list`, `session status` and the monitor.
3. `task show <id>` renders it marked removed.
4. `task list --removed` lists it.
5. **Id monotonicity.** Remove the highest task, add a new one, assert the new
   id is greater than the removed one. This is the regression the whole change
   exists to prevent.
6. `sessions.active_task_id` and `session_statuses.active_task_id` are nulled;
   `task_landings` rows survive.
7. Pending `session_notices` for the removed task are gone; delivered ones
   remain.
8. `task remove --cascade` marks every descendant and nulls every descendant's
   `active_task_id` pointers.
9. The E-1915 relation guard and E-1927 bulk-clear guard still refuse.
10. **Rebuild the DB from the db-ledger, then re-run 1, 2 and 5.** This is the
    check that catches an executor/projector divergence. Without it the change
    can look complete and still re-free every id on the next rebuild.

Scripting the rebuild inside the suite (step 10) is deliberate and untried. If
it turns out not to be safely automatable, split it out as a manual step and
record that in the manifest — do not drop the assertion.

Plus `just build && just test`.

fields.description: Three rules govern task content (extends E-1058's description policy and grounds E-1064's audit). (1) Analysis is pre-plan/pre-implementation design content only; once a task ships the analysis is historical record, so auditing it for currency is a category error. (2) NO durable content — description, analysis, text/plan, outcome, or a decision body — may include time-frozen specifics: byte counts, file sizes, line numbers, path:NNN citations, match counts, or sha hashes of moving artifacts. They have near-zero historical value and create false-precision drift, and a plan citing them is stale the moment anything else lands, which forces the implementing session to decide whether to override it and pushes that judgment onto the user. Cite durable identifiers instead — function, handler, command or symbol names — or better, state the SEARCH that finds the sites rather than the sites themselves. (3) When a task's plan fully documents the chosen design, analysis MUST NOT be NULLed; it is a historical record.

# Plan — E-1929: replace task deletion with a `removed` flag

Implements ED-1547 for tasks. `task remove` stops issuing a DELETE and marks the
row `removed = 1`, so the id can never be re-minted and the FK-free rows that
deliberately outlive their task can never resurrect against unrelated work.

Absorbs E-1930, E-1931 and E-1932 (all closed `obsolete`).

## Decisions this plan implements

Settled with the requester before filing; none of these are open.

| Question | Decision |
|---|---|
| FK actions that stop firing on removal | Split: explicitly null `sessions.active_task_id` and `session_statuses.active_task_id`; leave `task_landings` rows in place |
| `task.bulk_cleared` (`task import --replace`) | Retains too — one rule, no second orphaning path. Whether `task import` earns its keep at all is E-1933 |
| A removed task's visibility | `task show <id>` renders it marked removed; `task list --removed` lists them; invisible everywhere else |
| Scope | Tasks only. Decisions and sessions have no reachable delete path, and decisions are being merged back into tasks |
| Read-filter mechanism | New `live_tasks` view; rewrite the read sites to use it |

## Why the id can be re-minted today

The task-id allocator in `internal/events/executor.go` allocates with
`SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 FROM tasks`. Only the *highest* id is ever
re-freed — interior gaps are never refilled — so no historical backfill is
needed. Retaining the row keeps `MAX(id)` monotonic, which is the entire fix.

**The single most important constraint in this change: that allocation query
must keep reading `tasks`, never `live_tasks`.** Pointed at the view it would
stop seeing removed rows, `MAX(id)` would drop back, and ids would be reused
again — reintroducing the exact bug while appearing to fix it. The sibling
decision allocator in the same file has the same hazard; this plan does not
otherwise touch it.

## 1. Schema migration

New change file `internal/schema/changes/e-1929-add-tasks-removed.sql`, applied
at land time by `endless db apply-change`; the runner wraps it in
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` and records the `_schema_version` marker, so it runs once.

```sql
ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN removed INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS live_tasks AS
  SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE removed = 0;

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_tasks_removed ON tasks(removed);
```

Plus the one-shot data repair in §5, in the same transaction.

Per ED-1472 `schema.sql` is the single source of truth and must be edited to
declare the post-migration shape — the `removed` column on `tasks`, the
`live_tasks` view, and the index. The sandbox and tests build from `schema.sql`
and never apply change files, so a change file without the matching `schema.sql`
edit passes the migration and fails every fresh build.

`SELECT *` in the view is deliberate: it inherits future columns automatically.
If that proves fragile against `ALTER TABLE`, the fallback is an explicit column
list, which then has to be maintained alongside `schema.sql`.

## 2. Removal path — executor

`execTaskDeleted` in `internal/events/executor.go`.

Replace both DELETEs with UPDATEs:

- Non-cascade: `UPDATE tasks SET removed = 1 WHERE id = ?`
- Cascade: same `WITH RECURSIVE tree(id)` walk, `UPDATE tasks SET removed = 1
  WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM tree)`

Keep the existing `UPDATE tasks SET parent_id = NULL WHERE parent_id = ?`. Today
that re-roots the orphans; retaining the row would otherwise leave children
hanging off an invisible parent, so preserving it is what keeps the tree
readable.

Add what the FKs used to do and now will not:

```sql
UPDATE sessions         SET active_task_id = NULL WHERE active_task_id = ?;
UPDATE session_statuses SET active_task_id = NULL WHERE active_task_id = ?;
```

Both were `ON DELETE SET NULL`. A session left pointing at a removed task is
live state that would be a lie, and E-1856 shows `active_task_id` drift is not
hypothetical. Under `--cascade` these must run for every id in the tree, not
just the root.

`task_landings` was `ON DELETE CASCADE` and now simply will not fire. That is
the intended outcome — landing history is audit data, and the retained task row
is there to explain it. No code needed; note it in the change-file comment so a
future reader does not "fix" it.

Delete pending notices in the same path (absorbed E-1931):

```sql
DELETE FROM session_notices WHERE task_id = ? AND notified = 0;
```

Undelivered mail about a removed task is dead; filtering it on read would leave
it queued permanently. Delivered history is untouched. This is not an exception
to ED-1547 — a notice's own id is an internal row handle nobody refers to.

`execTaskBulkCleared` in the same file gets the identical treatment: its
`DELETE FROM tasks WHERE project_id = ? AND source_file = ?` becomes an UPDATE,
keeping its existing `parent_id` re-rooting. E-1915's reasoning applies — one
rule with no exemption beats two rules with a judgment call at the boundary.

The E-1915 relation guard and the E-1927 bulk-clear guard both stay exactly as
they are. Refusing to remove a task that still has relations is orthogonal to
how the removal is then recorded.

## 3. Removal path — projector

The `task.deleted` and `task.bulk_cleared` replay handlers in
`internal/events/projector.go` must be changed to match §2 exactly.

This is the rebuild path: it replays the whole ledger to rebuild the DB from
scratch. If the projector still replayed removal as a real DELETE while the
executor marked `removed = 1`, a rebuild would silently re-free every removed
id — the failure ED-1547 calls out by name, on a path nobody would think to
test. §6 verifies it explicitly.

## 4. Read-path rewrite

Point every read at `live_tasks`. Find the set — do not trust any list written
here, which is why this section states searches rather than locations:

- `FROM tasks` and `JOIN tasks`, across Go, Python and tests. This is the sweep.
- `UPDATE tasks`, `INSERT INTO tasks`, `DELETE FROM tasks` — the complement.
  These are writes and must NOT move; SQLite views are not writable.

The session-status reads are the ones that motivated E-1926: they join `tasks`
and today drop dangling references by accident. Retaining the row makes them
start matching, so they are where a missed rewrite leaks a removed task into
`session status` and the monitor. Find them by the sweep above; they are the
joins feeding the status and monitor renderers.

**Must NOT be rewritten** — each needs a comment saying why:

- The task-id allocator — the `COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 FROM tasks` query. See
  the boxed constraint above. This is the one that silently undoes the whole
  change, and it is the first thing to grep for.
- Every write, per the complement search above.
- The removal path itself (§2, §3) — it must see and set rows the view hides.
- `task show <id>` and `task list --removed` (§5).
- The §5 repair sweep.
- Anything under the schema `changes/` directory. Historical migrations are
  applied-once history, not live code; editing them rewrites the past.
- `reconcile`'s orphan detection, if its purpose is finding rows whose task is
  gone. Decide per call site while reading it.

## 5. CLI surface

`remove_item` in `src/endless/task_cmd.py` keeps its guards and messaging; only
the emitted effect changes. Reword its output from "deleted" to "removed" so the
CLI stops claiming something it no longer does.

`task show <id>` resolves against `tasks`, not `live_tasks`, and renders a
removed task with a clear marker. This is the payoff for retaining the row: an
id that is a hole explains itself instead of erroring.

`task list --removed` lists removed tasks, querying `tasks WHERE removed = 1`.
Define its interaction with the existing filters — simplest is that `--removed`
replaces the default live set rather than adding to it, so it never interleaves
removed and live rows in one listing.

**One-shot repair, absorbed from E-1932.** In the same migration transaction,
delete `session_tasks` rows that provably belong to a previous occupant of a
reused id — the row's timestamp predates its task's `created_at`:

```sql
DELETE FROM session_tasks
 WHERE id IN (
   SELECT st.id FROM session_tasks st
     JOIN tasks t ON t.id = st.task_id
    WHERE st.created_at < t.created_at
 );
```

Measured against the real ledger while planning, the affected set was small,
confined to session_tasks; the dangling rows whose task no longer exists are harmless — they are what "outlives its task" means, and are already
invisible through the view. Re-measure all four tables before running the sweep
rather than assuming that shape held.

## 6. Verification

A bespoke `tests/tasks/e-1929-verify.sh`, following the shape the prior verify
scripts use: a throwaway git repo as project root under a temp dir, with its own
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (hence its own DB and ledger) and `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, the
worktree's `bin/` prepended to `PATH` so the event bridge execs the candidate
binary, pass/fail per check with a summary, and exit 0 / 1 / 2 for
all-passed / any-failure / setup problem.

`verify.toml` is deliberately not used: that functionality has not landed.

The script must assert:

1. Remove a task — the row survives with `removed = 1`.
2. It is absent from `task list`, `session status` and the monitor.
3. `task show <id>` renders it marked removed.
4. `task list --removed` lists it.
5. **Id monotonicity.** Remove the highest task, add a new one, assert the new
   id is greater than the removed one. This is the regression the whole change
   exists to prevent.
6. `sessions.active_task_id` and `session_statuses.active_task_id` are nulled;
   `task_landings` rows survive.
7. Pending `session_notices` for the removed task are gone; delivered ones
   remain.
8. `task remove --cascade` marks every descendant and nulls every descendant's
   `active_task_id` pointers.
9. The E-1915 relation guard and E-1927 bulk-clear guard still refuse.
**Executor/projector parity — do NOT verify this by rebuilding a real DB.**

The hazard is real: if the projector still replays removal as a DELETE while the
executor marks `removed = 1`, a rebuild re-frees every removed id and the change
ships looking complete. But `rebuild-db` is not yet reliable, and the main DB is
canonical until it is (see the rebuild-reliability epic). A verify script that
rebuilds is both a risk to real data and a source of flaky failures attributable
to the rebuild rather than to this change.

Verify it instead with a Go test in the events package, following the existing
`TestProjectToTempDB_*` pattern: project a synthetic event stream —
`task.created`, then `task.deleted`, then a fresh `task.created` — into a temp
DB, and assert the removed row is present with `removed = 1` and that the new
task's id is greater than the removed one. That exercises the projector's
removal handler and the allocator against replayed state, in isolation, with no
real DB and no dependence on `rebuild-db` working end to end.

Add the same assertions for `task.bulk_cleared`.

Plus `just build && just test`.

payload.title: Make db-ledger rebuild reliable enough to trust over the main DB
payload.description: Today the main DB is canonical and rebuild-db is not trusted: a rebuild is neither robust nor reliable, so it must not be exercised against real data, and verify scripts have to route around it. That is a load-bearing gap — the ledger is supposed to be the source of truth the DB projects from, and E-1829's two-developer milestone depends on each developer rebuilding the projection from the shared ledger. Until rebuild is trustworthy, every executor handler has a projector twin that nothing exercises end to end, so divergence between them is invisible until someone rebuilds and loses data. Umbrella for the work that closes that gap: existing candidates include E-1671 and E-1674 (event upcasting so old events replay into the current schema), E-1728 (projector failing task_landings inserts), E-1716 (committed test-fixture ledger events), E-1883 (DB scoping so a rebuild is project-safe), and executor/projector parity testing in general. Relate or reparent those once the shape is agreed.

# Analysis

## Why this is being asked now

E-1898 rebuilt session→pane binding onto a `processes` table keyed on
`(kind, server_uuid, address)`, because the old `sessions.process` string (a
bare tmux pane id) is not unique across tmux server lifetimes — the root cause
of the 2026-08-05 incident that nulled live pane bindings project-wide.

`channels` keys on that SAME string (`INSERT INTO channels (process, port, pid,
created_at)`, `DELETE FROM channels WHERE process=?`, `SELECT port, pid FROM
channels WHERE process=?` — internal/monitor/session.go:274-308). E-1898
deliberately left it alone rather than migrate a surface believed dead, so
after E-1898 lands `channels` is the last consumer of the old non-unique key.

## The assumption that needs confirming first

"channels is vestigial" is Mike's read, and it may be wrong. The
`endless-channel` MCP server is still wired into live Claude sessions — its
instructions ship in the session system prompt:

    Events from Endless arrive as <channel source="endless-channel" ...>.
    When you see event_type="message", run: endless channel inbox

So the surface is at minimum still *installed*. Whether it is ever *exercised*
is the empirical question.

## What to brainstorm

1. **Confirm the premise.** Does anything read/write `channels`? Is the MCP
   server ever actually invoked? Check the ledger, the errors log, and whether
   any session has ever run `endless channel inbox` unprompted.

2. **Re-read the MCP standard.** It has changed recently; capabilities that
   were impossible when endless-channel was built may now be available.
   Reference Mike watched: https://youtube.com/watch?v=oqp6D-ugtX4

3. **Evaluate `SendMessage`.** Claude Code exposes a SendMessage tool that
   continues a previously spawned agent by ID/name with its context intact.
   That may be a better transport for inter-session communication than a
   bespoke MCP server plus a port/pid table — it needs no listener, no port
   allocation, and no process-keyed row that can go stale.

4. **Decide.** Three live options:
   - retire `channels` + the MCP server outright;
   - migrate `channels.process` onto `processes.process_id` (only worth it if
     the surface is genuinely used);
   - rebuild inter-session comms on SendMessage and retire the rest.

## Out of scope

Implementation. The outcome is a decision plus a follow-on retirement or
design task.

# E-1898 — liveness is observed, never inferred

## The one-sentence change

Delete the reaper. Give every pane binding an identity that is unique across
tmux server lifetimes, observe liveness into a temp table per unit of work, and
JOIN. No code path may conclude a session is dead by looking at tmux and then
writing that conclusion to the `sessions` table.

## Why the previous plan was replaced

The prior plan guarded the destructive write with an escalating series of gates
(server-uuid gate, peer-server enumeration, ordering guarantees, forced
override). Every gate was an inference about whether the pane set in front of
the process was the right one to judge by, because no row recorded which tmux
server it was bound to. Stacking gates narrows the window; it cannot close it,
and each gate added edge cases and un-mockable tmux tests.

Recording the binding's server identity removes the need for every one of those
gates. This plan is shorter than the one it replaces because the complexity was
compensation for a missing column, not essential difficulty.

## Invariants — these are the acceptance criteria

**I1 — No inferred destructive write.** No code path writes `state='ended'`, or
clears a pane binding, based on an observation of tmux. Only reported facts (a
`SessionEnd` hook) and explicit operator action close a session. There is no
sweep, no reaper, no mass UPDATE.

**I2 — Bounded blast radius.** A failed or incomplete observation may affect at
most the rows it actually observed. `unknown` is NEVER converted to `dead` by
any consumer. An unreachable server costs zero rows.

**I3 — Identity unique across server lifetimes.** A tmux pane id reused by a new
server can never match a binding made against the old one.

**I4 — Tests need no tmux server.** Liveness is a JOIN against a table; tests
seed that table directly. No private tmux servers, no socket enumeration, no
seam counters.

Verification drives each invariant explicitly. I1 and I2 are the ones this task
exists for; a change that satisfies I3 but not I1 has not fixed anything.

## Model

Multiplexer-agnostic. tmux is one populator; cmux and herdr add their own
without touching consumers.

```
process_kinds(id, slug)          -- tmux | pid | ...   (mirrors session_kinds)

processes(                       -- DURABLE identity. A fact, kept forever.
  id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  kind_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES process_kinds(id),
  server_uuid   TEXT,            -- tmux @server_uuid; NULL for kind=pid
  address       TEXT NOT NULL,   -- tmux pane id '%414'; or the pid as text
  os_pid        INTEGER,
  first_seen_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  last_seen_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE(kind_id, server_uuid, address)
)

sessions.process_id -> processes.id     -- replaces sessions.process

TEMP live_processes(kind_id, server_uuid, address, command, os_pid)
TEMP observed_servers(kind_id, server_uuid)   -- which servers we actually reached
```

`processes` is append-mostly: a row is created the first time a session binds to
an address on a server, and is never deleted by observation. A tmux restart
mints a new `@server_uuid`, therefore a new `processes` row, therefore I3 holds
structurally — not by a guard that could be wrong.

## Liveness — three-valued, derived at read

```sql
CASE
  WHEN o.server_uuid IS NULL           THEN 'unknown'  -- server not reached
  WHEN l.address IS NULL               THEN 'dead'     -- reached; pane absent
  WHEN l.command IN ('zsh','bash','sh','fish')
                                       THEN 'dead'     -- pane outlived its harness
  ELSE                                      'live'
END
FROM sessions s
JOIN processes p        ON p.id = s.process_id
LEFT JOIN observed_servers o USING (kind_id, server_uuid)
LEFT JOIN live_processes  l  USING (kind_id, server_uuid, address)
```

Expose as a view (`session_liveness`) so no consumer re-derives it.

`unknown` is the safe branch: render last-known, condemn nothing. Per I2, no
consumer may map it to `dead`. The site that needs care is the spawn/claim
ownership guard — under `unknown` it must assume STILL OWNED and refuse. A
wrong refusal is an annoyance; the inverse steals a live worktree.

The shell test is the E-1898 death-test insight kept, with its danger removed:
it is now a read-time classifier, never a kill criterion. Verified empirically
2026-08-09 — a live Claude pane reports its version string (`2.1.220`), even
mid-Bash-tool-call, so it does not collide with the shell set. Accepted residual:
Claude's startup window before the title is set can read `dead` for one
observation. Consequence is a briefly-wrong read, never a write.

## Snapshot population

Refresh at the start of each **unit of work** — a CLI/hook invocation, an HTTP
request, a monitor repaint — inside the transaction that reads it, so a single
statement never sees two different observations.

For tmux: list sockets in `dirname $(tmux display-message -p '#{socket_path}')`;
for each, read `@server_uuid` and, when present, one
`tmux -S <sock> list-panes -a -F '#{pane_id} #{pane_current_command} #{pane_pid}'`.
Each successfully-read server contributes a row to `observed_servers`.

Enumeration stays, but is no longer load-bearing for safety: a server we cannot
reach (`tmux -S` outside the socket dir, relocated `TMUX_TMPDIR`) yields
`unknown` for its rows, not a verdict. This is the entire difference from the
previous plan's peer-enumeration gate, which had to be complete to be safe.

## Binding: where server_uuid comes from

The hook runs inside the pane. It reads `@server_uuid`; if absent it generates
and stamps one, exactly as `tmux init` does. Every binding therefore carries a
real server identity, and the previous plan's "refuse when uninitialized" gate
is unnecessary — identity is always present rather than sometimes checked.

## Deleted

- `monitor.ReapDeadTmuxPanes` and `internal/monitor/reap.go`, including the
  `len(alive) == 0` mass-UPDATE that ended every tmux row in one statement.
- `runInit`'s `runReset(nil)` call — the documented trigger for the 37-row batch.
- `endless tmux reset` as a destructive verb. Retained read-only as
  `endless tmux status`, printing the liveness view. Nothing to force.
- `TouchSession`'s collision invalidation. A reused pane is a different
  `processes` row, so the pane-reuse case cannot arise; a genuine same-server
  collision leaves both rows and the reader orders by `last_activity`.
- From the previous plan: D1, D2, D5, D6, D9 and their tests. D3's insight is
  kept as a read-time classifier; D7 and D8 survive as below.

## Kept from the previous plan

- **D7** — `runInit` no longer reaps (now: there is nothing to reap).
- **D8** — `runStatusLine` records a fault instead of silently rendering the
  placeholder on error. One correction to that decision: because
  `faults.Bind` is wired to `monitor.DB` (main.go:144) and `faults.Record`
  swallows its own DB failure by contract, this covers the non-DB fail-closed
  exits, not all of them. Worth doing; do not claim full coverage.
- The **ledger-safety assertion** in the verify suite.

## Migration

1. Create `process_kinds`, `processes`, add `sessions.process_id`.
2. Backfill: one `processes` row per distinct non-null `sessions.process`, with
   `server_uuid = NULL` (the binding server is not knowable retroactively) and
   `kind` derived from the string shape (`%N` -> tmux, `pid:N` -> pid).
   Those rows read `unknown` — safe by I2 — and self-heal to a real
   `server_uuid` on the session's next hook. Existing live sessions therefore
   recover within seconds without any repair verb.
3. Convert the ~35 call sites comparing `process` to a raw pane id. The type
   changes, so a missed site is a COMPILE ERROR — the property that made this
   safe to do where string-encoding `<uuid>:<pane>` would not have been.
4. Drop `sessions.process`.

`channels` is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE and keeps its string key; see E-1936.
It becomes the last consumer of the old key, deliberately, pending that
brainstorm's decision on whether it should exist at all.

## Tests — `tests/tasks/e-1898-verify.sh`

**Layer A — liveness truth table (FAIL-FAST, pure SQL fixtures, no tmux).**
Seed `processes`, `sessions`, `live_processes`, `observed_servers` directly and
assert every cell: server unobserved -> `unknown`; observed + present + claude ->
`live`; observed + absent -> `dead`; observed + present + shell -> `dead`. Same
pane id under two different `server_uuid`s resolves independently (I3).

**Layer B — invariants as tests, not as prose.**
- **I1:** grep the tree for any write of `state='ended'` or a binding clear
  outside the SessionEnd path; assert zero. Then drive a full hook cycle against
  an EMPTY `live_processes` (the exact 2026-08-05 shape: observer sees nothing)
  and assert **zero rows changed**. This is the regression test for the incident.
- **I2:** with `observed_servers` empty, assert no row reads `dead` and the
  ownership guard refuses rather than freeing.
- **I4:** the whole of A and B runs with `tmux` absent from `$PATH`.

**Layer C — one E2E** against a private tmux server (`-f /dev/null`, throwaway
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`) proving the populator fills the snapshot from a real server.
Exactly one, because the logic under test is now SQL, not tmux plumbing.

**Layer D — project-wide regression:** `go test ./...`, `just test`, `just build`.

**Ledger-safety assertion (mandatory).** Count non-ended sessions holding a
binding in the REAL database before and after the suite; they must be equal.

## Out of scope

- `channels` and the `endless-channel` MCP server (E-1936).
- Idle-timeout / session-duration truthfulness. Positive observation covers
  "Claude died, pane lives" without inferring death from silence.
- Non-tmux (`pid:`) liveness. The model has a slot for it; no populator ships here.
- Repairing rows damaged on 2026-08-05. Repaired by hand; migration step 2
  heals the rest on the next hook.

triage.rationale: The task explicitly asks to brainstorm among three unresolved options (retire, migrate, or rebuild on SendMessage) without stating which to pursue or on what basis to decide.

Recording the binding's server identity removes the need for every one of those
gates. This plan is shorter than the one it replaces because the complexity was
compensation for a missing column, not essential difficulty.

## Invariants — these are the acceptance criteria

**I1 — No inferred destructive write.** No code path writes `state='ended'`, or
clears a pane binding, based on an observation of tmux. Only reported facts (a
`SessionEnd` hook) and explicit operator action close a session. There is no
sweep, no reaper, no mass UPDATE.

**I2 — Bounded blast radius.** A failed or incomplete observation may affect at
most the rows it actually observed. `unknown` is NEVER converted to `dead` by
any consumer. An unreachable server costs zero rows.

**I3 — Identity unique across server lifetimes.** A tmux pane id reused by a new
server can never match a binding made against the old one.

**I4 — Tests need no tmux server.** Liveness is a JOIN against a table; tests
seed that table directly. No private tmux servers, no socket enumeration, no
seam counters.

Verification drives each invariant explicitly. I1 and I2 are the ones this task
exists for; a change that satisfies I3 but not I1 has not fixed anything.

## Model

Multiplexer-agnostic. tmux is one populator; cmux and herdr add their own
without touching consumers.

```
process_kinds(id, slug)          -- tmux | pid | ...   (mirrors session_kinds)

processes(                       -- DURABLE identity. A fact, kept forever.
  id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  kind_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES process_kinds(id),
  server_uuid   TEXT,            -- tmux @server_uuid; NULL for kind=pid
  address       TEXT NOT NULL,   -- tmux pane id '%414'; or the pid as text
  first_seen_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  last_seen_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE(kind_id, server_uuid, address)
)

sessions.process_id -> processes.id     -- replaces sessions.process

TEMP live_processes(kind_id, server_uuid, address, command)
TEMP observed_servers(kind_id, server_uuid)   -- which servers we actually reached
```

`processes` is append-mostly: a row is created the first time a session binds to
an address on a server, and is never deleted by observation. A tmux restart
mints a new `@server_uuid`, therefore a new `processes` row, therefore I3 holds
structurally — not by a guard that could be wrong.

## Liveness — three-valued, derived at read

```sql
CASE
  WHEN o.server_uuid IS NULL  THEN 'unknown'  -- server not reached
  WHEN l.address IS NULL      THEN 'dead'     -- reached; address absent
  ELSE                             'live'
END
FROM sessions s
JOIN processes p             ON p.id = s.process_id
LEFT JOIN observed_servers o USING (kind_id, server_uuid)
LEFT JOIN live_processes  l  USING (kind_id, server_uuid, address)
```

Expose as a view (`session_liveness`) so no consumer re-derives it.

Liveness is now PURELY OBSERVATIONAL: "is this address present on a server we
actually reached?" There is no remaining inference in it. That is the property
that makes I1 and I2 checkable rather than argued.

`unknown` is the safe branch: render last-known, condemn nothing. Per I2, no
consumer may map it to `dead`. The site that needs care is the spawn/claim
ownership guard — under `unknown` it must assume STILL OWNED and refuse. A
wrong refusal is an annoyance; the inverse steals a live worktree.

### Why the shell test is NOT part of liveness

The previous plan's death test was "address absent OR the pane runs a known
shell", to catch a killed harness whose pane survives. It is dropped from
liveness, because it is an inference and it can be wrong about a LIVE session:

- Verified 2026-08-09: a live Claude pane reports its version string
  (`2.1.220`) as `pane_current_command`, even mid-Bash-tool-call. So it does
  not collide with the shell set during normal operation.
- But **Ctrl+Z** puts the shell back in the foreground. A suspended-but-alive
  Claude session's pane reports `zsh`. Under the shell test that session reads
  `dead`, which drops its status line to the placeholder and — the part that
  matters — lets the spawn/claim ownership guard treat its task as free and
  hand the worktree to another session.

Cost of dropping it: a harness killed with its pane still open (SIGKILL, no
SessionEnd) leaves a stale-`live` row until the pane closes. That is a wrong
read in the SAFE direction — a refusal, never a theft — and E-1807's actual
case had a dead pane, which address-absence still catches.

`live_processes.command` is still collected, but is used ONLY for the cosmetic
"pane is running Claude but has no session row" status-line hint. An inference
is acceptable for a hint that misleads nobody and owns nothing; it is not
acceptable for liveness. That line is the rule, and the code must not blur it.

## Snapshot population

Refresh at the start of each **unit of work** — a CLI/hook invocation, an HTTP
request, a monitor repaint — inside the transaction that reads it, so a single
statement never sees two different observations.

For tmux: list sockets in `dirname $(tmux display-message -p '#{socket_path}')`;

Enumeration stays, but is no longer load-bearing for safety: a server we cannot
reach (`tmux -S` outside the socket dir, relocated `TMUX_TMPDIR`) yields

previous plan's peer-enumeration gate, which had to be complete to be safe.

The hook runs inside the pane. It reads `@server_uuid`; if absent it generates
and stamps one, exactly as `tmux init` does. Every binding therefore carries a
real server identity, and the previous plan's "refuse when uninitialized" gate
is unnecessary — identity is always present rather than sometimes checked.

fields.title: Generate on-disk markdown for external tools that require it
fields.description: Parked. If a tool Endless must work alongside requires markdown files on disk in prescribed locations, Endless needs to render ledger content out to those files. Generation and sync only — the event-sourced document entity this epic originally proposed is obsolete, since brainstorm tasks took over the evolving-design role documents were meant to fill. Revive against a concrete external tool, which will specify the requirement better than this placeholder.
fields.text:
# Documents on disk for external tools

## What is parked here

Only one thing: if a tool Endless has to work alongside requires markdown files
on disk in prescribed locations, Endless needs a way to keep those files current
without a human re-typing content that already lives in the ledger.

That is a generation-and-sync problem — one authoritative source rendered out to
one or more files — and nothing more. It does not need a document entity, event
kinds, section identifiers, Lexorank ordering, a proposal/review workflow, or
conflict surfacing.

## Why the original epic died

The epic was written to solve design-doc drift: ask an AI to revise a design
document and it regenerates the whole document instead of evolving the existing
one, leaving two versions that partly agree and require manual reconciliation.
The proposed fix was documents as event-sourced entities peer to tasks, with
section-level events making whole-document regeneration structurally impossible.

Brainstorm tasks solved that problem by another route. A brainstorm task is a
topic whose thinking evolves in place across sessions, in a field the tooling
already treats as authoritative, under a lifecycle that already has human review
in it. That is what the document entity was for. Once brainstorms existed, the
section-level event machinery had no problem left to solve, and every child of
this epic was obsoleted.

Two children died for reasons of their own as well. The dashboard views die with
the decision to rewrite the web surface from scratch. The ADR workflow lost to
decisions as a capability, whose storage shape is being re-decided under E-1868.

## What would revive this

A concrete external tool that reads markdown from a fixed path, where the
content it needs is already maintained in Endless. When that shows up, the tool
specifies the requirement — file layout, section conventions, refresh trigger —
far better than this placeholder can, so the right move is a fresh task written
against that tool rather than reopening the shape sketched here.

The in-repo precedent for what the mechanism would look like is the canonical
status-lifecycle mermaid block, which is duplicated byte-identically across
several documentation files and held in sync by a verification script rather
than by generation. That pattern generalizes: one source, rendered out, checked
at land time.

## Superseded design

`docs/private/endless-documents-design.md` describes the abandoned approach. It
is retained as a record of the reasoning, not as a spec. Its analysis of the
drift problem still holds; its proposed mechanism does not.

Also inherits the disposition of ED-907, which asserts decisions-on-tasks is a temporary shim 'until E-801/E-841 (documents system + ADR workflow)' - both now obsolete, and this epic makes decisions-on-tasks the destination rather than the shim, so ED-907 needs reconsidering or superseding once the mechanism is settled.
